evidence.label: Metric Markov Cotype Two of ℓ1

headline: Claims to prove that ℓ1 has metric Markov cotype two, settling Ball's extension problem for maps into ℓ1.
scope: The real Banach space ℓ1, with constant N₂(ℓ1) at most 12√21, and Lipschitz maps from subsets of real Hilbert space into ℓ1.
plain: Metric Markov cotype asks whether points on a random walk can be nudged to make each step short, at a cost set by longer stretches. Mendel and Naor asked whether the space ℓ1 has this property with exponent two. This paper claims yes, with a constant at most 12√21. As a result, Lipschitz maps from any subset of Hilbert space into ℓ1 would extend to the whole space with a fixed loss. There is no Lean check.
doesNot: This does not extend to every subspace of ℓ1: a known closed subspace still fails metric Markov cotype at every finite exponent.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Keith Ball, who introduced Markov type and cotype to study Lipschitz extension
scorecard.significanceWhy: If correct, it answers a question of Mendel and Naor and resolves Ball's extension problem for maps into ℓ1.

explanation:
Toss three independent coins, each landing heads with chance 0.3. What is the chance that most of them show heads? It is 3 × 0.3² × 0.7 + 0.3³, which equals 0.189 + 0.027 = 0.216. In general, the chance is 3h² − 2h³ when each coin shows heads with chance h. This small formula, a "majority of three" rule, is the heart of this paper.

The setting is the space ℓ1. Its points are infinite lists of numbers whose absolute values have a finite sum. The distance between two lists is the sum of the absolute differences of their entries. Take a Markov chain, a random walk on finitely many states that moves by fixed chances. Call it reversible if it looks the same run backward. Put a point x_i of the space at each state i. Metric Markov cotype two asks for new points y_i with two properties. Each step between new points is short. And the total cost of moving from x to y is small. Both must be paid for by how far the original points spread over t steps, up to a fixed constant[2].

Keith Ball introduced Markov type and cotype to study when Lipschitz maps extend[3]. A Lipschitz map stretches distances by at most a fixed factor. His linear version of cotype fails for ℓ1[4]. Mendel and Naor gave the metric form and asked whether ℓ1 has it[5]. One obstacle was a known example. Using a construction of Kalton, they found a subspace of ℓ1 that fails metric Markov cotype at every exponent[6]. So the new points must be allowed to leave any subspace that holds the data.

The paper claims that ℓ1 does have metric Markov cotype two[1]. Its constant N₂(ℓ1) is at most 12√21, about 54.99. Squared, that is 144 × 21 = 3,024[7]. The proof writes finitely many points of ℓ1 as weighted cuts, which are 0-or-1 coordinates. It runs the walk for a random number of steps, with mean t. It then applies the rule φ(r) = 3r² − 2r³ to each coordinate. The slope of φ is zero at 0 and at 1, which keeps the steps small[8]. Each new point y_i turns out to be the average coordinatewise middle value of three random walk endpoints that start at i[9].

The main consequence concerns Ball's extension problem[10]. It asks whether a Lipschitz map from any subset of Hilbert space into ℓ1 extends to the whole space with only a fixed loss. Hilbert space is the infinite-dimensional version of ordinary Euclidean space. Mendel and Naor showed earlier that a yes to their question gives such an extension. So, if the proof holds, the answer is yes.

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The paper says its main proof is elementary and does not rely on extension theorems. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if correct: it would close a question of Mendel and Naor and Ball's extension problem for ℓ1. There is no Lean check and no published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: The space of infinite lists of numbers whose absolute values have a finite sum, with distance the sum of absolute differences.
A random walk on a set of states where each move depends only on the current state.
A chain whose statistics look the same when run backward.
A property: points on any reversible walk can be moved so each step is short, at a cost bounded by longer-range spread.
A map that stretches every distance by at most a fixed factor.
An infinite-dimensional version of ordinary Euclidean space, with lengths and angles.
A split of a finite set of points into two parts, used here as a 0-or-1 coordinate.
